screens.title: Scripting Audio Playback in Unity
screens.subtitle: Control AudioSource from C# to make game audio responsive and expressive

narration.text: In this chapter we move beyond Inspector setup and into dynamic, script-driven audio. You will learn how to trigger sounds precisely when events occur, how to avoid common issues that mute or cut off effects, and how to shape sound in real time by adjusting volume and pitch. We’ll show concrete scripts for playing single clips, layering rapid sound effects without interruption, and making looping sounds respond to simulated game variables such as speed. You’ll also practice a hands-on activity that implements footsteps and a door interaction so you can hear these techniques in a simple scene. By the end of the lesson you’ll be able to decide when to use Play, PlayOneShot, Pause, or Stop, and how to wire AudioSource references safely in the Inspector. Notice one common pitfall: calling Play on a source that’s already playing restarts the clip, which can make rapid effects sound wrong. Throughout, I’ll point out debugging checks like null-reference guards and sensible defaults so your audio behaves consistently. Ready to build responsive game audio that reacts to gameplay and avoids typical mistakes?

keyIdea.title: Why script audio?
keyIdea.text: Scripting gives precise, event-driven control. It lets you layer sounds, change pitch and volume at runtime, and respond to game events reliably.

screens.title: Why script audio instead of only using the Inspector
screens.subtitle: Understand the limitations of static setup and the benefits of dynamic control

narration.text: Using the Inspector to assign AudioSource components and clips is quick and reliable for static looping music or ambient tracks. But many game sounds must respond to events, player actions, or changing game state, and Inspector-only setup cannot react at runtime. Scripting lets you trigger sounds exactly when an event happens, adjust properties like pitch and volume based on variables, and layer short effects without creating many temporary objects. For example, when a player picks up multiple items quickly, you want each pickup sound to play cleanly even if the same AudioSource is already playing; PlayOneShot solves that. Another practical benefit is stateful control: Pause preserves the clip position, Stop resets it, and Play resumes or restarts depending on context. A common misconception is that you must create a new AudioSource for every overlapping sound; in most cases, PlayOneShot lets a single source handle many short effects. In short, scripting audio turns static clips into responsive feedback tied to gameplay, which improves player clarity and immersion. screens.title: Core playback methods: Play, Stop, Pause
screens.subtitle: How each method behaves and when to use it

narration.text: Three basic methods control an AudioSource: Play, Stop, and Pause. Play begins or resumes playback of the assigned clip. But Play has an important behavior to remember: if the source is already playing the assigned clip, calling Play restarts it from the beginning. That restart is useful for sounds you always want to begin fresh, like a UI click, but it is a poor choice for rapid, overlapping effects. Stop immediately stops the clip and resets the playback position to the start. Use Stop when you want a sound to cancel and reset, such as aborting a charging sound when an ability is canceled. Pause freezes the clip at its current position; a subsequent Play resumes from where it left off. This makes Pause useful for temporary interruptions like pausing the game or temporarily silencing a looping ambience. A common mistake is to mix Play and PlayOneShot incorrectly: use Play for long, looping, or resumable clips and PlayOneShot for short, overlapping effects. When scripting, always check for null references before calling these methods to avoid runtime errors. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Play / Stop / Pause
Playback semantics
  1. Play() — starts or resumes the assigned clip; restarts if already playing the same clip.
  2. Stop() — stops playback and resets position to start.
  3. Pause() — pauses at current position; Play() resumes from there.
Quick rule

Use Play for loops and resumable audio; Stop to cancel; Pause for temporary holds like menu or cutscenes.

Common pitfall

Calling Play on repeating short clips will repeatedly restart them, producing audible clipping. For short, repeatable SFX, prefer PlayOneShot.

Example scenario

When the player presses jump, you may want the jump sound to start fresh every press. Using Play on a dedicated jump AudioSource is fine. But if multiple jumps happen rapidly and should overlap, PlayOneShot is better.

Key Takeaway

Match method to intended behavior: restart, cancel, or pause.

screens.title: Play() versus PlayOneShot()
screens.subtitle: Why PlayOneShot is essential for overlapping short effects

narration.text: A crucial distinction in Unity audio is between Play and PlayOneShot. Play plays the AudioSource's assigned clip and will restart that clip if invoked while it's already playing. That restart behavior is sometimes desired, but it makes Play unsuitable for short, rapid, or overlapping sounds. PlayOneShot takes an AudioClip as an argument and plays it immediately without changing the AudioSource. clip or stopping any clip that is already playing. This allows multiple instances of the same short effect to overlap cleanly, which is essential for sound types like rapid gunfire, stacked footsteps, or quick UI blips. Another advantage is resource efficiency: PlayOneShot avoids creating and destroying temporary AudioSource objects when many short sounds occur. A common misconception is that PlayOneShot always plays at full volume; in fact it accepts a volumeScale parameter so you can layer quieter or louder instances. When designing your audio system, use Play for music and long loops, and PlayOneShot for overlapping short SFX. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Play vs PlayOneShot
Play()

Plays the assigned clip on the AudioSource. If already playing, Play restarts the clip from the beginning.

Good for:
  • Looped music
  • Resumable ambient sounds
  • One-shot actions where restart is intended
PlayOneShot()

Plays a provided AudioClip immediately without stopping or replacing the AudioSource's current clip, allowing overlap.

Good for:
  • Rapid-fire effects like gunshots
  • Multiple footsteps in quick succession
  • Layered UI blips
Concrete example
If a machine gun fires while another shot is still playing, PlayOneShot allows each "bang" to be heard separately. Using Play would restart the clip on each shot, making the result choppy.

narration.text: Let's step through a common PlayerAudioController pattern that assigns an AudioSource and plays assigned clips for actions like jumping or picking up items. The code also includes a PlayPickupSound method that other scripts can call when an item is collected. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › PlayerAudioController
Example script
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerAudioController : MonoBehaviour
{
    public AudioSource playerAudioSource; // Assign in Inspector
    public AudioClip pickupSound;         // Assign in Inspector
    public AudioClip jumpSound;           // Assign in Inspector

    void Update()
    {
        // Example: Play jump sound on spacebar press
        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
        {
            if (jumpSound != null)
            {
                playerAudioSource.clip = jumpSound; // Assign the jump sound
                playerAudioSource.Play();           // Play it
            }
        }
    }

    // This method could be called by an item's script when picked up
    public void PlayPickupSound()
    {
        if (pickupSound != null)
        {
            playerAudioSource.clip = pickupSound;
            playerAudioSource.Play();
        }
    }
}
Key points
  • Public fields let you wire components in the Inspector.
  • Assigning clip then calling Play restarts that clip.
  • Use PlayOneShot instead when pickups can overlap rapidly.
  • Always check for nulls: audioSource and audioClip may be unassigned.
Misconception

Assigning clip at runtime is flexible, but it changes the AudioSource.clip which may be used elsewhere. Consider PlayOneShot to avoid replacing the assigned clip.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › PlayOneShot Example
WeaponAudio snippet
using UnityEngine;

public class WeaponAudio : MonoBehaviour
{
    public AudioSource weaponAudioSource; // Assign in Inspector
    public AudioClip shootSound;          // Assign in Inspector
    public AudioClip reloadSound;         // Assign in Inspector

    void Update()
    {
        if (Input.GetMouseButtonDown(0)) // Left click to shoot
        {
            if (shootSound != null)
            {
                weaponAudioSource.PlayOneShot(shootSound);
            }
        }

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.R)) // R key to reload
        {
            if (reloadSound != null)
            {
                weaponAudioSource.PlayOneShot(reloadSound);
            }
        }
    }
}
Practical notes
  • PlayOneShot avoids changing the AudioSource.clip, keeping persistent loops intact.
  • Use volumeScale to lower repetitive sounds, e.g., PlayOneShot(clip, 0.7f).
  • Randomize small pitch offsets for natural variation: audioSource.pitch = 1f + Random.Range(-0.05f,0.05f).
Key Takeaway

PlayOneShot is the efficient, simple way to layer short SFX on a single AudioSource.

narration.text: This hands-on example combines movement-driven footsteps and a door toggle. The script exposes an AudioSource and arrays of footstep clips so you can assign different terrain sounds. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Footsteps & Door
PlayerMovementAndInteraction
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerMovementAndInteraction : MonoBehaviour
{
    public AudioSource playerAudioSource; // Assign this in Inspector
    public AudioClip[] footstepSounds;    // Assign different footstep clips here
    public AudioClip doorOpenSound;       // Assign door open clip
    public AudioClip doorCloseSound;      // Assign door close clip

    public float moveSpeed = 5f;
    public float footstepInterval = 0.5f; // Time between footsteps
    private float nextFootstepTime;

    private bool doorIsOpen = false; // State for the door

    void Start()
    {
        if (playerAudioSource == null)
        {
            playerAudioSource = GetComponent();
            if (playerAudioSource == null)
            {
                Debug.LogError("Player AudioSource not found on this GameObject!", this);
            }
        }
        nextFootstepTime = Time.time;
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // --- Player Movement (for footsteps) ---
        float horizontalInput = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
        float verticalInput = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

        Vector3 movement = new Vector3(horizontalInput, 0, verticalInput) * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime;
        transform.Translate(movement, Space.World);

        // Play footstep if moving and enough time has passed
        if (movement.magnitude > 0.01f && Time.time >= nextFootstepTime)
        {
            PlayFootstepSound();
            nextFootstepTime = Time.time + footstepInterval;
        }

        // --- Door Interaction ---
        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.E)) // Press 'E' to interact with door
        {
            ToggleDoor();
        }
    }

    void PlayFootstepSound()
    {
        if (footstepSounds.Length > 0 && playerAudioSource != null)
        {
            AudioClip randomFootstep = footstepSounds[Random.Range(0, footstepSounds.Length)];
            playerAudioSource.PlayOneShot(randomFootstep, 0.7f);
        }
    }

    void ToggleDoor()
    {
        if (playerAudioSource != null)
        {
            if (doorIsOpen)
            {
                if (doorCloseSound != null)
                {
                    playerAudioSource.PlayOneShot(doorCloseSound);
                    Debug.Log("Door Closing Sound Played!");
                }
            }
            else
            {
                if (doorOpenSound != null)
                {
                    playerAudioSource.PlayOneShot(doorOpenSound);
                    Debug.Log("Door Opening Sound Played!");
                }
            }
            doorIsOpen = !doorIsOpen; // Toggle the door state
        }
    }
}
Testing checklist
  • Assign AudioSource and clips in Inspector before Play mode.
  • Move the capsule and confirm footstep timing and variation.
  • Press 'E' to toggle door and verify open/close sounds play and log messages appear.
Key Takeaway

PlayOneShot provides reliable, overlapping playback for footsteps and interactions without changing the assigned clip.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Pitch & Volume
DynamicEngineSound
using UnityEngine;

public class DynamicEngineSound : MonoBehaviour
{
    public AudioSource engineAudioSource;
    public float minPitch = 0.8f;
    public float maxPitch = 1.5f;
    public float minVolume = 0.3f;
    public float maxVolume = 1.0f;

    // Assume 'speed' is a variable controlled by your vehicle's movement script
    public float currentSpeed = 0f; // This would come from actual vehicle physics

    void Update()
    {
        // Simulate speed change for demonstration
        currentSpeed = Mathf.Sin(Time.time) * 0.5f + 0.5f; // Oscillates between 0 and 1

        // Map speed to pitch and volume
        engineAudioSource.pitch = Mathf.Lerp(minPitch, maxPitch, currentSpeed);
        engineAudioSource.volume = Mathf.Lerp(minVolume, maxVolume, currentSpeed);

        // Ensure engine sound is playing
        if (!engineAudioSource.isPlaying)
        {
            engineAudioSource.Play();
        }
    }
}
Practical notes
  • Smooth transitions to avoid clicks: interpolate changes over time.
  • Keep pitch in a small band to maintain natural timbre.
  • Combine subtle volume and pitch changes for realism rather than extreme shifts.
Example

Map vehicle speed to pitch to make the engine feel responsive as speed increases, then test and tweak the min/max to taste.

screens.title: Event-driven audio patterns
screens.subtitle: Triggering audio from collisions, triggers, and input

narration.text: Event-driven audio means sounds are played in direct response to gameplay triggers like collisions, triggers, or player input. Typical Unity events are OnCollisionEnter, OnTriggerEnter, and input checks in Update. For example, when a player collides with a pickup, the pickup script can call a method on the player's audio controller to play a pickup sound. This keeps audio logic modular: the collision object only signals that an event occurred, and a centralized audio handler decides how to play the associated sound. A common trap is tightly coupling audio calls to physics code; instead prefer calling a public audio method so you can change the playback strategy later. Also, handle rate limiting for events that may fire rapidly — use cooldown timers or PlayOneShot to avoid overwhelming a single AudioSource. Event-driven audio improves clarity because sound directly corresponds to actions, but it requires consistent wiring and null checks so missing references don't break gameplay. Event-driven audio patterns means emit events from gameplay and call audio methods that decide when and how to play sounds, keeping concerns separated and testable.. screens.title: Designing AudioSource placement
screens.subtitle: Local vs centralized AudioSources and when to use each

narration.text: Deciding where to place AudioSources affects spatialization, layering, and maintenance. A localized AudioSource on a player GameObject is ideal for spatialized sounds like footsteps and engine hum, where position and 3D rolloff matter. Centralized sources — for example a SoundManager — work well for UI sounds, global music, or shared one-shot effects that do not require individual spatial positions. A hybrid approach is often best: keep spatial sounds local and non-spatial or UI sounds centralized. Architecturally, minimize the number of AudioSource components you create dynamically; prefer PlayOneShot on an existing source to avoid instantiating many temporary objects. Another concern is mixing: centralized sources can simplify global volume control for music and UI. Finally, document your placement decisions and keep an audio policy for the project so team members know whether to attach sounds locally or use the manager. This saves debugging time and prevents inconsistent audio behavior across scenes. Designing AudioSource placement means use local audiosources for spatial, position-sensitive sounds and centralized sources for ui/music; combine approaches for clarity and efficiency.. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › AudioSource Architecture
Local AudioSources

Attach to GameObjects for spatialized effects such as footsteps, weapon sounds, or engine hum. Spatial blend should be set to 3D for local sources.

Pros
  • Natural 3D positioning
  • Independent control per object
Centralized AudioSources

Use a SoundManager for UI, music, and shared effects. Keep a small set of global sources and prefer PlayOneShot to layer short effects efficiently.

Pros
  • Consistent global control
  • Simpler volume and mute handling
Recommendation

Use hybrids: spatial local sources for positional sounds and a central manager for UI and music. Document the policy for your team.

narration.text: Many audio bugs are simple to diagnose with a consistent checklist. First, check Inspector assignments: public AudioSource and AudioClip fields must be populated or guarded by code that obtains defaults. If a sound does not play, confirm the AudioSource component exists and is enabled, the clip is assigned (or passed to PlayOneShot), and the volume and spatial settings allow audible output. Second, avoid using Play for overlapping short effects; this frequently produces choppy audio. Third, watch for excessive pitch changes that distort the clip — small ranges are safer. Fourth, use Debug. Log messages around audio calls during testing to confirm the code path runs and the clip variables are non-null. Fifth, test in both editor and build configurations because audio settings or compression may differ. Finally, when performance matters, reuse AudioSources and prefer PlayOneShot instead of instantiating many temporary GameObjects. Following these steps will make audio behavior more predictable and easier to tune. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Debugging & Mistakes
Common mistakes and how to fix them
  • Missing references: confirm AudioSource and AudioClip assignments or use GetComponent fallback.
  • Wrong method: Play used where PlayOneShot is appropriate.
  • Too extreme pitch: small pitch ranges avoid distortion.
  • Performance: reuse AudioSources and avoid creating many temporary objects.
Mistake

Calling Play repeatedly for short SFX makes them cut each other off.

Fix

Use PlayOneShot or separate channels for intended overlap.

narration.text: These three concepts capture essential behaviors you will use every session. First, AudioSource. Play() starts or resumes the assigned clip but will restart it if already playing, so use it for loops and resumable audio. Second, AudioSource. PlayOneShot() plays a supplied clip without stopping the source’s current clip, enabling overlapping short effects like gunfire or footsteps. Third, AudioSource. Pause() preserves position while Stop() resets playback. Understanding these differences helps you choose the right call for the desired audio behavior. Keep these concepts in mind while wiring and testing your audio so sounds behave predictably during gameplay. AudioSource.Play()
Starts or restarts the assigned clip; good for loops and resumable audio.
PlayOneShot()
Plays a clip without stopping current clips on the same AudioSource, enabling overlap.
Pause / Stop
Pause preserves position; Stop halts and resets to the start.
Summary

Choose the method that matches whether you want restart, overlap, pause/resume, or cancel semantics.

narration.text: These final three concepts tie implementation details to design and debugging. First, audio properties like volume and pitch are scriptable at runtime; mapping variables with Mathf. Lerp makes sounds reflect game state such as speed. Second, prefer event-driven audio: emit events from gameplay elements and let audio handlers decide playback to keep code modular and testable. Third, debugging often requires simple checks: confirm Inspector assignments, add null guards, log playback calls during testing, and choose PlayOneShot to avoid overlap bugs.
